abstract: Methanol is emerging as a sustainable and energy-dense one carbon (C1) feedstock for next-generation biomanufacturing, owing to its superior energy density, abundance, water miscibility, and decoupling from food supply chains. Methylobacterium species are facultative methylotrophs that have evolved sophisticated metabolic and regulatory networks for efficient methanol utilization. This review highlights the transition of Methylobacterium from a model organism for dissecting methylotrophy to a programmable C1 chassis for synthetic biology. We provide a unique overview of its core metabolic architecture, focusing on the lanthanide-switchable pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ)-dependent methanol oxidation, the tetrahydromethanopterin (H₄MPT)-mediated formaldehyde buffering system, and the tight coupling of the serine cycle with the ethylmalonyl-CoA (EMC) pathway, which together govern carbon flux, redox balance, and energy efficiency. Building on this intrinsic framework, we survey how these traits are leveraged to produce high-value chemicals, such as folate derivatives, redox cofactors, organic acids, terpenoids, bioplastics, and single-cell protein. Furthermore, we discuss advanced engineering strategies for systematic chassis optimization including global transcriptional regulation, metabolic valve control, and photo-methylotrophic configurations, along with a comprehensive evaluation of Methylobacterium chassis advantages and disadvantages, concrete product-chassis matching rules, common engineering bottlenecks, and diversified low-cost feedstock options. Finally, we propose a product-chassis matching framework and outline future directions centered on regulatory control, flux coordination, and robustness enhancement to overcome current limitations in titer, yield, and scale-up, while also leveraging agricultural applications and low-cost feedstocks, thereby positioning Methylobacterium as a cornerstone of sustainable low-carbon biotechnology.
